notes.h: Reasons poverty continues in modern western society
notes.b: Poverty persists where income from work is low or missing and where the costs of living absorb whatever income there is. The reasons fall into economic ones, about money and jobs, and social ones, about family, health and society.
points: Unemployment: a household with no earned income depends on State payments, which are normally lower than wages, so it has less to live on. Recession and high unemployment are the usual first reason given.
Long-term unemployment erodes skills, work habits and confidence, which makes re-entry to the labour market (the pool of available jobs) harder the longer it lasts.
Low pay: unskilled and minimum-wage work, and part-time or insecure work, often leaves full-time workers unable to afford an acceptable standard of living. These are called the working poor.
Limited education: early school leavers and people with few qualifications or skills are concentrated in low-paid and insecure work, or in no work at all.
Lone parenthood and large families: one income must cover food, housing and childcare for several people, and childcare costs can stop a lone parent working at all.
High housing and living costs: rent, mortgage repayments, a shortage of affordable housing, energy, transport and childcare take a large share of low incomes, so little is left for other needs.

Social problems: addiction and gambling divert money from essentials and lead to debt, for example when spending on alcohol, drugs or gambling replaces spending on food or heating. Ill health and disability can also stop people working.

Economic change: recession and industrial decline mean the closure of a major employer removes jobs and the local businesses that depended on its workers' spending. Globalisation (production moved abroad) and automation (production mechanised) reduce demand for unskilled labour, mainly in manufacturing.
Inequality in society: wealth and power are unequally shared, and some groups face discrimination, which limits their access to jobs, housing and services.
notes.tip: When a question asks for social and economic reasons, group them: economic are unemployment, low pay, recession and high costs; social are family structure, addiction, the cycle of poverty and the poverty trap. Explain each reason rather than just naming it.

notes.h: The cycle of poverty (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Disadvantage is passed from one generation to the next, so poverty repeats itself unless something interrupts the pattern. The cycle of poverty is poverty handed from parents to children through limited education, work and income.
points: Children raised in low-income households often have less access to good education, health care and social networks than children from better-off families, as well as poorer housing and diet.
Disadvantage such as poor study conditions, low expectations and financial pressure can lead these children to leave school early with few qualifications, and then into unemployment or low-paid work.
Their own children are then born into the same financial conditions, so the pattern repeats across generations.
Each stage reinforces the next: low income means poorer housing and diet, which affect health and school attendance, which in turn limit qualifications and later earnings.
Breaking the cycle requires action at a weak point where it repeats, for example early-years education, family support and access to training and employment.
notes.tip: Give the cycle as a sequence of stages, not a single sentence. Examiners ask for it separately from the cycle of deprivation and the poverty trap, so do not blur them.

notes.h: Influence of social policy on poverty (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Social policy is the set of State decisions on welfare payments, housing, education, health, minimum pay and employment. These decisions affect how many people are poor and for how long.
points: These decisions determine who is poor and for how long, because they set the income, housing and training available to each household.
Policy can reduce poverty through welfare payments, the national minimum wage, free or subsidised health care, housing supports and education measures for disadvantaged areas.
A minimum wage sets a legal floor for pay, so it directly determines what a full-time low-paid worker earns.

Policy can also keep people poor if it is inadequate or badly designed. Critics argue that welfare payments set below the cost of basic needs keep recipients in poverty, and that a gap between welfare and wages is a problem.
Social policy can perpetuate poverty where losing benefits when a person takes a job makes low-paid work financially unattractive.
Other critics argue that generous payments reduce the incentive to seek work and so sustain dependence on the State. This is a contested view, so present it as a criticism.

Housing policy affects poverty directly: the supply and cost of social and private rented housing decide how much of a low income is left after rent, and a failure to supply affordable homes keeps people poor.
Support that is poorly targeted or changes often leaves gaps, so families move in and out of poverty rather than escaping it.
notes.tip: Show that policy can both reduce poverty and keep people poor. A strong answer on the cycle of poverty and social policy gives one developed point on each, using the loss of benefits that makes low-paid work unattractive.

notes.h: Cycle of deprivation in families and geographical areas (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Deprivation is the lack of resources, services and opportunities that are normal in society. The cycle of deprivation is the way deprivation across several areas of life together, income, education, housing, health and services, reinforces itself and is passed on.
points: In families, low income, low education and ill health limit the support parents can give children for learning, and children inherit the same limits.
Children in such families often have little contact with people in employment, so they grow up with few examples of working life and low expectations, and repeat the pattern.

In geographical areas, unemployment, welfare dependence and poor housing are concentrated in the same place, creating employment blackspots, often after a major industry closes. Some disadvantaged urban estates and some rural areas are examples.
Services in those areas, such as shops, buses, schools and health centres, close as spending falls, and the area gets a poor reputation, making it less attractive to employers and families.
Deprivation reinforces itself: an area losing population, employers and skilled workers loses the tax base and local spending that could sustain new employment.
Responses must work on the place as well as the household, for example community development, community education, transport, local training, job creation and local services.
notes.tip: Keep this separate from the cycle of poverty: the cycle of deprivation is multiple deprivation reinforcing itself in a family or an area. Name the group (family or area) and develop each point.

notes.b: The poverty trap is a situation in which taking up work brings little or no gain in net income, so a person stays on welfare. It is a problem of benefit withdrawal.
points: A person on welfare who takes a low-paid job loses benefits or supports, and may pay tax and PRSI, so net income (what they keep) rises little or not at all, and may even fall. They can be no better off than on welfare.
Supports often withdrawn as earnings rise include housing assistance, a medical card and, in some cases, child-related payments.
The costs of working, such as transport, childcare and work clothing, reduce the gain further.
When welfare is financially more rewarding than low-paid work, people have little incentive to take employment, which keeps them dependent on welfare.

Payments reduced gradually as earnings rise, rather than withdrawn all at once, lessen the trap. In-work payments such as the Working Family Payment, a tax-free weekly payment for low-paid working parents, are designed to help low-paid working families.
notes.tip: Give the trap with an example: loss of a medical card or other supports plus the costs of working leave a person no better off in a low-paid job than on welfare.

notes.h: Effects of poverty on the individual
notes.b: Poverty affects a person's mind, health and place in society, and these effects can then make it harder to escape poverty.
points: Stress, worry and fear about money can lead to depression and poor mental health.
Loss of status and self-esteem, and a feeling of worthlessness, can reduce confidence to seek work or training.
Social isolation and exclusion, because the cost of leisure, travel and social activities is beyond reach.
Poor diet, and poorly heated or damp housing, increase the risk of illness, and ill health can prevent people from working.
Some people turn to alcohol, drugs or gambling as a means of escape, which adds to debt and poverty.
notes.tip: For effects, name the group (individual, family, child) before each effect, and explain each effect rather than just listing it.

notes.h: Effects of poverty on families and children
notes.b: When a household cannot meet its basic needs, the strain falls on the whole family, and children can carry the effects into adult life.
points: Families may be unable to afford adequate food, clothing, heating and housing, and fall into rent, mortgage or utility arrears and debt. In the worst cases, they lose their home and become homeless.
Financial pressure increases conflict and relationship strain, and can contribute to family breakdown.
Children may be unable to take part in school trips, sport, clubs or activities their peers attend, which leads to embarrassment and affects belonging and self-esteem.
Children without a quiet place to study, books or internet access may fall behind in school, and poor diet and health can affect their concentration.
Children growing up in poverty are more likely to leave school early with few qualifications, which limits their later earnings and risks poverty as adults, the cycle of poverty.
Poorer diet and access to health care can affect children's physical health and development.
Loss of a home forces children to move school and loses the stability that supports their learning.
notes.tip: On effects on families and children, give a list of effects each with a short explanation, naming whether it affects the family or the child.

notes.h: Effects of poverty on the community and the State
notes.b: Poverty does not stay within households. Where it is concentrated, it affects whole neighbourhoods and the public finances.
points: Higher demand for welfare, health and housing services increases the cost to the State.
Concentrated poverty can contribute to crime, anti-social behaviour and vandalism in an area.
Falling spending in poorer areas leads to shop closures and fewer local services, which reduces jobs further.
Poverty reduces the skills and productive capacity available to the economy, because people who are unemployed or poorly educated cannot contribute fully.

keyTerms.definition: The process by which disadvantage, such as low education and income, is passed from one generation to the next and repeats.
The reinforcing process in which a lack of resources, services and opportunities in families or areas causes further disadvantage.
A situation in which moving from welfare into low-paid work brings little or no gain in net income because supports are withdrawn.
The State's decisions on welfare, housing, pay, education and employment, which shape who is poor and for how long.
The lack of resources, services and opportunities that are normal in society, and the exclusion that results.
An area with persistently high unemployment, often where a major industry has closed.
Being unable to take part in activities considered normal in society because of low income and limited resources.

factCards.term: Four reasons poverty continues in modern western society
factCards.definition: Unemployment and low pay; limited education and qualifications; high housing and living costs; lone parenthood and large families relying on one income.

factCards.term: Three effects of poverty on children
factCards.definition: Early school leaving with few qualifications; poorer health and development; low self-esteem and reduced participation in school life.

factCards.term: Costs that can cancel out the gain from low-paid work
factCards.definition: Transport, childcare and work clothing, plus the loss of supports such as housing assistance or a medical card.

factCards.term: Two ways disadvantage reinforces itself within families and areas
factCards.definition: Within families, disadvantage passes from parents to children through limited support for learning and work; within areas, concentrated unemployment and closing services reinforce each other.

factCards.term: Effect of poverty on family finances
factCards.definition: Rent, mortgage, utility and credit arrears build up when income cannot cover essential bills.

factCards.term: Signs that an area has concentrated joblessness and decline
factCards.definition: Persistently high unemployment, long-term welfare dependence and the closure of a major local employer or industry.

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by the poverty trap and describe one way it discourages people from taking up work.
questions.model: The poverty trap is a situation in which moving from welfare into work brings little or no gain in net income. Earnings from low-paid work cause payments or supports to be withdrawn. Supports that may be lost include housing assistance and medical card eligibility. The extra costs of working, such as childcare and travel, reduce the gain further. Because welfare can be financially more rewarding than low-paid work, people have little incentive to take up employment and remain dependent on the State.

questions.prompt: Examine why poverty persists in modern western societies, and assess how the cycle of deprivation and social policy contribute to it.
questions.model: Reasons for persistence: unemployment and low pay leave households without adequate income; limited education and qualifications restrict people to insecure work; high housing and living costs absorb low incomes; lone parenthood and large families depend on one income; addiction and debt drain resources; recession and industrial decline remove jobs; globalisation and automation reduce demand for unskilled labour. Cycle of deprivation: in families, low income and low education limit the support parents give children, who inherit the same disadvantage; in geographical areas, concentrated unemployment and dependence on welfare create employment blackspots, and closing services reduce the area's attractiveness, which deepens decline. Social policy: welfare payments set below the cost of basic needs can keep recipients in poverty, while generous payments are criticised for reducing the incentive to work; the minimum wage sets the floor for low pay; housing policy determines the rent burden; the poverty trap arises when withdrawal of supports offsets earnings; policy that is poorly targeted or changes often leaves families moving in and out of poverty. Assessment: the cycle of deprivation and social policy interact, since policy can either break or reinforce the cycle through education, housing and employment supports.
